This goes back 35 years ago when people were certain industry incumbents were lobbying for copyright protection for computer programs. speaker: Mr. Paul Goldstein

speaker: REPUBLIC OF KOREA

Building on Mr. Kim Yong-Sun’s remarks, allow me to offer three observations from Korea’s experience. First, human contribution and responsibility must remain central. Under Korea’s guidelines on AI assisted inventions, a human must make a substantial contribution to the invention to be recognized as an inventor.

speaker: REPUBLIC OF KOREA
text: An output generated by AI alone is not sufficient. The same principle should guide the use of AI within IP offices. AI can assist IP professionals, but legal judgments and final decisions must remain under meaningful human oversight. Second, AI should contribute not only to efficiency but also to the quality and integrity of the IP system. As AI lowers barriers to filing, IP offices face growing and application volumes and new challenges concerning the quality of applications.

speaker: REPUBLIC OF KOREA
text: Korea is responding through early screening measures and by piloting AI-powered patent search system, they can better understand the meaning and the technical context of patent documents. Third, successful AI transformation requires not only new tools but also new capabilities within IP offices. Korea has launched an internal AI app store through which staff can develop and share AI applications tailored to their work. This initiative demonstrates that successful transformation depends not only on technology but also on people, skills, trust, and organizational readiness. Mr. Chair, the national experiences shared at this forum reflect different practices but also common priorities they have made clear that no country or IP office can address these challenges alone.

speaker: REPUBLIC OF KOREA
text: The Republic of Korea supports WIPO’s leadership in developing shared principles for responsible AI use while respecting the different circumstances of IP offices. We also hope that WIPO will continue to serve as a global platform for practical cooperation and mutual learning. Finally, the we express our appreciation to the WIPO Secretariat, especially the IP and Frontier Technologies Division of the Infrastructure and Platform Sector for its dedicated efforts in making this forum possible. Thank you. Thank you very much.

speaker: REPUBLIC OF KOREA

Going forward in the legal global copyright discussions led by WIPO, the Republic of Korea sincerely believes that the essential elements of human creation should be treated in a technology-neutral manner, even amid swift technological innovations including artificial intelligence. Last but not least, the Republic of Korea would like to bring WIPO’s attention to various legal debates arising from mass acquisition of printed books for AI training which seem to have been occurring in many Member States including the Republic of Korea. The Republic of Korea hopes that meaningful discussion will take place among Member States within WIPO, which is the most authoritative forum for this agenda. Thank you very much, Chair.

speaker: REPUBLIC OF KOREA
text: Thank you very much. Then I would like to call Mr. Matsuo Nonaka, Deputy Commissioner, Japan Patent Office. Japan, you have the floor. Thank you again. Japan Patent Office would like to express its sincere appreciation to the WIPO Secretariat for organizing this first global forum on IP and AI.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Over the past two days, one message has become even clearer to me.

speaker: JAPAN
text: The impact of AI is reaching every aspect of our economy and society and the pace of change continues to accelerate. The scale of this transformation is presenting significant challenges as well as opportunities for the Intellectual Property system. We had many perspectives on a wide range of issues, how to promote both the protection and the use of data needed for AI, how to balance AI development and adoption with the fair distribution of its benefits, how differing national interests and stakeholder perspectives can be reconciled and even how AI may fundamentally reshape the principles of the IP system and the role of IP offices themselves. While it may be difficult to reach a common understanding on all of these issues today, I believe it is a very important achievement that the key challenges have been comprehensively identified and that such valuable experiences and insights have been shared at the high level. At the same time, as I would like to emphasize one point, AI development is not only rapid, it is accelerating.

speaker: JAPAN
text: What we consider a common understanding today may no longer be a common understanding tomorrow. Therefore, to keep pace with these rapid developments, we must continue to examine with a sense of urgency how the IP system should evolve to support global innovation and creativity and how IP offices should adapt to this changing environment. Director General Tan reminded us that this may no longer be a moment for safe conversations, for wait and see or business as usual. I share that view. As human beings, we naturally tend to prefer familiar approaches and established practices.

speaker: JAPAN
text: That is the reason why strong leadership and high level commitment to change are essential. In that regard, I believe this global forum has provided an excellent opportunity for all of us to recognize not only the need for change but also the need to begin that change today. Finally, as AI continues to evolve, I hope that WIPO will continue to provide opportunities like this forum so that we can learn from one another, work together, and respond to further development in a coordinated and timely manner. I thank you very much. Thank you very much.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Now I would like to call Mr. Gavin Hu, head of copyright unit and the principal legal counsel, Intellectual Property Office of Singapore, IPOS. You have the floor. Thank you, ADG. text: Over these two days, we have explored a wide spectrum of AI issues across IP rights, IP systems, and IP offices. speaker: SINGAPORE
text: In charting the way ahead, Singapore reaffirms our commitment to engaging and collaborating internationally, including through the various WIPO Standing Committees. speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Now I would like to call Ms. Gaelu Umtani, lead of Rwanda’s responsible AI office, Rwanda, joining remotely. I have been informed that she is not online. speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Dear forum participants, dear colleagues, first of all, allow me to express my gratitude to the World Intellectual Property Organization for organizing this important international dialogue.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: It is dedicated to the interaction between artificial intelligence and Intellectual Property. As we are well aware, Artificial Intelligence is irreversible. Its influence today to a greater or lesser extent extends to the majority of areas of our lives. However, from the perspective of Intellectual Property, at the center of this transformation are the fields of creativity and law. Artificial Intelligence is one of the greatest technological breakthroughs.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: It is changing the face of civilization. And together with big data analytics, it simultaneously poses serious challenges. The main feature of autonomous Artificial Intelligence is the ability to produce results without direct human creative involvement. For example, in its specific case, Generative Artificial Intelligence learns from huge datasets and creates texts, music, images and videos which if created by a human would typically be protected by copyright. Currently, a human centered approach is legally and doctrinally accepted meaning that only a human can be the author or rights holder and within this approach there are indeed different opinions.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: The spectrum of views ranges from the assumption that such content falls into the public domain which is fully consistent with current legislation. That is, free use of the works. However, it is still subject to criticism as it acts as an obstacle to the development of new technologies. So how can the activities of Artificial Intelligence be regulated by law? The solution to this problem naturally can be approached from two perspectives.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: One is the Delegate, meaning the existing legislation and the other is the Delegate, meaning the delegated authority, that is, desirable or necessary legislation. Let’s start with the Delegate. The current legislation is in effect. It does not recognize Artificial Intelligence as a legal subject and it transfers, you could say, the rights to the physical persons who are related to the object. Legal protection has been established autonomously.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: However, the results remain problematic because recognizing any user request which is called a prompt as an act of creativity leads to the devaluation of the concept of creative work. An equally important question is the legality of using protected works. This is for training Artificial Intelligence without the consent of the copyright holder. There are differing opinions regarding the regime of legal protection. For example, protections similar to that of derivative works or photographic works or works that have no authors, such as the transmission by an organization of broadcast or cable television, noncreative databases, sound recordings, know-how or by analogy, including the topologies of integrated microchips as well as the recognition of objects as works made for hire and objects protected under a special sui generis regime, another fundamentally different option is the recognition of authorship of

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: a work created by Artificial Intelligence and the existence of rights for the subject of that activity. This can and should be implemented only within the framework of desirable legislation. Unlike the anthropocentric approach, this approach is electron centric. Obviously, it contradicts existing legislation. However, even if we were to accept this hypothetical possibility, we will see that such a rights holder can only have the right of authorship and the right to name.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: The other rights simply make no sense. And they cannot have property rights. The essence of these rights is either material benefit or legal liability for actions. In other words, even in the hypothetical case mentioned, legal capacity will be limited. There is also an approach based on hybrid authorship, that is, when both Artificial Intelligence and a human are recognized as coauthors.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: However, its implementation will require adding an additional clause to the legislation providing for the possibility of such coauthorship. In this case, the legal capacity of Artificial Intelligence will still be limited. And such a work must be excluded from the list of copyright objects. And this approach is applied in the United States of America. Now, a few words about algorithmization and associative thinking because this is closely related to the concept of the legal capacity of Artificial Intelligence.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: Algorithmization implies automated data processing and the search for solutions based on computational algorithms. Whereas human thinking relies on associative connections, intuition, memory and personal experience. Associative connections form associative memory. In humans, unlike humans, Artificial Intelligence does not have consciousness. It does not experience emotions.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: And it has no personal experience or memories that belong to a human being. As a result, statistics replaces intuition because the machine is looking for mathematical patterns not meaning ultimately modern fuzzy neural networks operate on the basis of mathematics and statistics. Relying on these, Artificial Intelligence does not think but rather simulates thinking. The human brain is not oriented towards computational enumeration but towards associative comparison or comparison with an imperfectly defined standard. This is a fundamental difference.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: It is of particular importance when evaluating the creative activity of Artificial Intelligence. It also relates to determining its possible legal subjectivity. What are the main difficulties in determining legal subjectivity? The problem encompasses three interrelated aspects. The first is philosophical.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: It involves rethinking the criteria for legal subjectivity, namely consciousness, reason and social necessity as well as possible recognition of a third category Artificial Intelligence. This is the distinction between a thing and a legal person. It involves legally reconciling authorship with rights, duties and liability. This includes the possibility of recognizing electronic entities. And in terms of praxology, the distribution of rights, risk insurance, licensing and mechanisms of responsibility, what changes are possible within the framework of desirable legislation that is in the event of a Lego forendum?

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: Over time, of course, a stage is possible where applications will be accepted and in cases where they are not submitted under the authorship of Artificial Intelligence with the distribution of rights among creators, owners and users. In our opinion, the mechanism for protecting copyright is very convenient by analogy with the protection of noncreative assets and the establishment of rights for electronic entities, the use of a neighboring rights mechanism is also possible. If initially Artificial Intelligence is not recognized as a full-fledged electronic entity, then in the distant future, as its participation in the economy becomes more active, it is quite possible that there will be a review and Artificial Intelligence will be granted. More comprehensive rights as a subject. The use of protection is also quite possible with the introduction of graduated levels of legal subjectivity of Artificial Intelligence practically starting from zero when Artificial Intelligence exists simply as an object, up to limited rights for specific legal actions.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: What does all this depend on? It all depends on philosophical and ontological discussions and on a rethinking of what makes us human beings as subjects of law. Biology, consciousness, reason or social necessity. And also on how Artificial Intelligence technologies themselves will manifest. What decisions related to Artificial Intelligence are desirable given the existing legislation?

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: I emphasize given the existing legislation. First of all, it seems advisable to develop a special international protocol similar to the Rome Convention on related rights which would regulate the rights and status of content created by Artificial Intelligence, separate from traditional copyrighted works. Secondly, it seems desirable to allow the use of protected materials for training Artificial Intelligence for commercial and research purposes provided that fair compensation is maintained by analogy with private copying such as making a copy. Thirdly, it seems advisable to establish a special protection regime for digital works created autonomously. This includes a limited term of protection from 25 to 30 years.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: In addition to this, there is another possible solution. It is the creation of a system of mandatory licensing. This would involve directing a certain portion of payments towards the use of content created by Artificial Intelligence. Funds to support human creativity. So, generative Artificial Intelligence, autonomous Artificial Intelligence and Artificial Intelligence in general, they have not created the problem of inefficiency in Intellectual Property and specifically copyright.

speaker: AZERBAIJAN
text: However, they have significantly exacerbated it, leading to a crisis situation. The further development of the legal system must be based not only on preserving existing principles but also on creating new legal mechanisms and if necessary, the necessity and new models of legal subjectivity. In all of this, in a world where Artificial Intelligence is bringing about a revolution, technology is a tool that requires human control. Thank you for your attention. Thank you very much.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Then I would like to call Ms. Kelly Sims, Acting Deputy Director General, Office of Director General, IP Australia. You have the floor. Thank you. Australia greatly appreciates the WIPO team, DG Tang and all of the speakers at this informative global forum on IP and AI.

speaker: AUSTRALIA
text: We have appreciated the discussions with other Member States and experts over the past two days. IP offices around the world are harnessing AI themselves and adapting their customers’ use of it as well. For Australia, this highlights the importance of maintaining two conversations in parallel. The first is the policy conversation about how IP frameworks respond to technological change and the second is the operational conversation about how IP offices can responsibly deploy AI to improve services, strengthen productivity and support users of the IP system.

speaker: AUSTRALIA
text: Australia has found that practical implementation raises issues that extend well beyond the technology itself. Trust, governance, transparency, workforce capability and human oversight are just as important as the tools. As more offices deploy AI, we see significant value in sharing experiences, lessons learned, best practices and approaches to governance. We also see value in continuing international dialogue about the role of AI within the IP system while we also recognize that technologies and national approaches continue to evolve. The pace of technological change means none of us have all the answers.

speaker: AUSTRALIA
text: What we do have is a shared interest and shared stewardship in ensuring that Intellectual Property systems remain trusted, effective and capable of supporting innovation and creativity in a rapidly changing world. We look forward to continuing these conversations with the WIPO community. Thank you. Sorry, it is still the interpretation is still ongoing. Thank you very much.

speaker: LAS (League of Arab States)
text: Now I would like to call His Excellency Henry Elie Monceau, Ambassador and permanent representative, Organization International de la Francophonie. Ambassador, you have the floor. You have the floor. Deputy Director General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen ambassadors, I would like to thank the World Organization for Intellectual Property for taking the initiative to hold this first forum. It opens an indispensable dialogue at a time when artificial intelligence is transforming not only creation but also our relationship with knowledge.

speaker: LAS (League of Arab States)
text: For it is itself a producer of knowledge. The Francophonie has always defended the rights of creators. They must be respected in the context of AI as elsewhere. Transparency regarding the use of works, consent, fair compensation. But I want to emphasize an issue that we consider a priority, linguistic and cultural diversity of the content that feeds AI.

speaker: LAS (League of Arab States)
text: The UNESCO convention of 2005 which the Francophonie among others helped to establish reminds us that cultural goods do not be just like any other commodity. This is already evident on the Web. According to the work of the Observatory of Linguistic and Cultural Diversity on the Internet, Haitian Creole is understood by 95% of Haitians but it appears on less than 8% of HT websites.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Rundi is understood by 98% of Burundians and it is the only language spoken and understood by more than 80% of the population. However, it is present on less than 1% of buy websites. This is not insignificant. More than 80% of the training data for these models is in a single language, English. And it is estimated that only 5% of the more than 7,000 living languages recorded have a sufficient digital footprint to be represented in AI in the long run.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: A language absent from the Web is absent from AI and with it, the knowledge it carries. An AI that only knows Africa or Asia through the eyes of others cannot reflect the real world. We talk a lot about open models but an open model that doesn’t understand my language remains to me a closed model. For a Bambara-speaking entrepreneur in a small town in Mali or an artist who expresses themselves in Fulani in Lome, if they cannot work in their own language, openness remains a promise on paper. Protection of rights and data diversity reinforce each other and it is in this spirit that the Francophonie recently brought together in Alexandria decision makers, AI entrepreneurs, data specialists and librarians.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: And their conclusions will, of course, be shared with the Secretariat of PIME. We invite them to participate in the follow-up. We call for three directions. First, to measure. We need tools and methods to measure the presence of languages and cultures in training corpora and thus open the black boxes they represent.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: No AI should be called inclusive unless we measure its language proficiency, the language proficiency of those it claims to serve. Second, encourage alternative solutions, smaller, more targeted, transparent models based on locally produced data. This requires supporting digitization while respecting the rights of the content from spaces that are currently underrepresented. Third, finally, to cooperate between the OMP, UNESCO and the linguistic spaces. The Francophonie is, of course, ready to contribute actively to this.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Now I would like to call Ms. Simantani Sharma, legal manager, Asia Pacific broadcasting union. You have the floor. I’m afraid the microphone is not yet ready.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Thank you, Chair. I speak on behalf of Asia Pacific broadcasting union, the world’s largest broadcasting union. I would like to add an important observation from the broadcasting sector. When we discuss AI and IP, there is sometimes a tendency to consider individual questions separately, which is the status of training material, the protection of a model, the use of AI in creating content and the rights in the resulting output. For broadcasters, these questions can arise within a single production and across several jurisdictions.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: That makes legal clarity particularly important. It is not only a question of determining whether a particular use is permissible. Organizations, especially public service broadcasters also need to understand how rights and responsibilities move through the different stages of the AI enabled production and distribution process. This is especially relevant in the Asia Pacific region where broadcasters operate across very different legal, technological and economic environment. I therefore think an important part of the continuing IP discussions is to look at these issues across the value chain rather than treating each question as an isolated legal problem.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Now let me move on to Mr. Ed Ryan, member Intellectual Property Owners Association who will join us remotely. You have the floor. Thank you.

text: IPO believes there is a role for WIPO in building upon this discussion and providing a forum for offices to provide specific information about the AI tools that they are using, how they are measuring the success of these tools and their policies regarding tool use by examiners. text: The discussion over the two days demonstrates both the opportunities presented by Artificial Intelligence and the challenges it poses for the creative sectors. speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Now I would like to call Mr. Roy Meltzer, Patent Attorney AI, AIPPI. You have the floor. Thank you, Chair. I speak on behalf of AIPPI which brings together IP practitioners from around the world. The Director General opened the forum with Venice, IP as the institution that moves value from the mind of the inventor into the economy.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: For centuries practitioners did exactly that. We took an idea and we turned it into value through the IP rights. Today alongside with that patent practitioners take on a new responsibility. The idea often reach us already processed by AI and AI is very generous. Asks to describe one invention and you get 40 fluffy pages, 12 embodiments and the short history of the wheel.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Somewhere inside usually around page 27 hides the actual innovation and it is our role to extract it. The inventor is human and it is the human inventor we represent. Our new responsibility is extraction and crystallization, finding the inventor own contribution inside all of the noise, separating it from the machine speculation and make sure that the real that it is real and enabled. Ideally we do it before the AI enters the picture so that as asked human judgment is recorded and not lost. This responsibility brings three challenges.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: First, transparency. Clients need to know how AI is used on their confidential matters and offices and courts will increasingly ask where the human contribution is. Practitioners are best placed to document it. If we rebuild and we have to build this habit now. Second, accountability.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: An AI model does not sign a filing. We do. As Mr. Ito put it, no one can stand up and say the AI thought it was a good idea. As we learned from Korea, they told us that patent filing by individual rose by 130% in the first half of this year alongside with a rise of low quality AI generated applications. speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: And third, training. Singapore told us that new examiners are asked not to use AI for four months and admitted that this does not really happen. We face the same problem. speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Otherwise as the filmmaker on the authorship panel feared we will get practitioner who draft like AI with no vision and no skill. The IP offices told us it all comes down to people. I would like to thank our capable Chair, Ambassador Toribayev for his excellent Chairpersonship and I’m delighted to share that the participation numbers has been extraordinary. On day one alone yesterday we were joined by over 2500 participants in the room or on Zoom and on the webcast. This is phenomenal.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: That is a remarkable response to a first-time event and a clear indication of the relevance of our discussions. Of course, bringing together so many people and launching something that has never been done before takes a tremendous amount of work behind the scenes which brings me to my sincere appreciation for the entire WIPO family as well as you for making this first forum possible. I’m sure that it is not a single part of WIPO that has not been involved in bringing these two days to you. From diplomatic engagement to conference services, from our regional divisions and external offices to our substantive sectors such as patents, trademark, design and copyright, from the print shop and security to the colleagues organizing side events and our communications and media teams helping us reach all of you around the world. And many, many others working behind the scenes.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: Accommodating our sometimes unusual requests, even at the last minute, finding solution to unexpected challenges, helping us think outside of the box, the support we have received from colleagues across the organization has been extraordinary. Thank you so much. I particularly want to give a special shoutout to our IP and front end technology division who is sitting besides me and also in the seats. The team at the heart of WIPO’s AI work who has poured its heart and soul into making the forum happen, working incredibly hard over the past several months, literally day and night. A special word of appreciation also goes to our tech team who are sitting over there as well who helped us introduce AI powered interpretation, not speak too fast but not too slowly and captioning in 20 languages at this forum.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: It seemed only fitting that we should put AI to work ourselves at the forum about AI. And I think the experience has been rather good illustration of both the opportunities and the challenges we have been discussing. Thank you so much. Was it perfect? I would say no.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: We discovered that humans can still manage to break some of the systems, AI systems, and we had to restart our systems more than a few times. But we also reached many more people in many more languages than would otherwise have been possible. So this was an achievement. This is what innovation within the UN system can look like, not simply taking about new technologies but testing them, learning from them, and using them to serve people better. At the opening, the Director General invited us to reflect on some fundamental questions about the future of Intellectual Property in the age of AI and the place of human beings in an increasingly AI driven world.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: AI is expanding the boundaries of what we can achieve, but it is also challenging some of our assumptions about creativity, innovation, ownership, and responsibility. Over those two days, we have explored those questions from many different perspectives. We also time-traveled back to WIPO’s first AI and IP symposium in 1991, reminding us something important. I was already born by that time. The IP system has faced major technological transformations before.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: Copyright has evolved through photography, radio, television, film, the Internet and streaming, and it will need to evolve again. But the speed and the space of AI means that we cannot simply assume that the approaches of the past will always be sufficient. Whatever the outcome of ongoing legal cases around the world, I would like to return to a point made by the Director General at the opening. As a global community, we should seek common ground and principles that can guide us as AI continues to develop. That does not mean we need to agree on every rule or that every country must take the same approach.

speaker: AIPPI (International Association For The Protection Of Intellectual Property)
text: Our legal systems, economic circumstances, and policy priorities will differ, which is reality. But we should be able to build shared understanding around some fundamental questions. How do we ensure that creators and innovators continue to be recognized and rewarded? How do we support the development and responsible use of AI? How do we make sure that the opportunities of this technology are accessible to countries, businesses, and communities around the world everywhere?

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: And how do we ensure that the IP system itself remains relevant, accessible, and effective for the next generation? The answers will not come from legal rules alone. We will also need new business models, licensing approaches, industry practices, and perhaps new ways of delivering IP services. We must remain open to adopting not only what the systems protect but also how it works for people who depend on it. And through all of these challenges, one principle must remain firm, namely, technology must humanity, not the other way around.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Ladies and gentlemen, colleagues and friends, through this forum makes an important new chapter in WIPO, WIPO’s engagement with these issues. Since its launch back in 2019, the WIPO conversation on IP and front-end technology has brought together nearly to 20,000 participants. This inaugural global forum builds on that foundation, responding to the growing demand for more focused member state-driven engagement on AI and IP. Let me close with one final thought. If there is one thing those two days have demonstrated, it is that the future of AI and Intellectual Property cannot be shaped from a single perspective.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: We need the voices of policy makers and judges, creators and innovators, researchers and businesses, technologists and communities from every part of the world. And we need to keep listening to one another, especially when do not disagree. Because the purpose of this forum was never to settle every question in two days. It was to create a space where we can ask the right questions, challenge our assumptions and to begin finding common ground. I believe we made a very good start.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Thank you all for being part of it, for those traveling back to home later today or tomorrow. I wish you safe travels. For those of you who are going to stay beyond today, you are very much welcome to join another event which is the first annual public meeting of WIPO’s artificial intelligence infrastructure interchange. Either way, we are already looking forward to welcoming you to the next WIPO’s global forum possibly in 2027 as mentioned by many colleagues in the panel on the floor. Thank you very much.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Now the meeting is adjourned. One quick announcement, housekeeping announcement. The colleagues before we conclude one final invitation, we would be grateful if you would join us for the reception immediately after this following just outside of the room, the lobby of the main building. We will also enjoy a musical performance by Noemi Beza, a Swiss singer/songwriter. Thank you very much all and look forward to seeing you at the reception in two minutes.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: Thank you.
